harder.updated_question: Research on ‘The role of ESG factors in stimulating countries' financial development’ with econometrics, where the dependent variables are: Financial Development Index, Financial Institution Index, Financial Market Index.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer includes at least one specific econometric model specification (e.g., fixed effects, random effects, GMM, panel regression) that explicitly defines ESG factors as independent variables and at least one of the three financial development indices as the dependent variable.

attempts.answer:
Below is a research roadmap and synthesis on how ESG factors stimulate countries’ financial development, with econometric design tailored to three dependent variables—Financial Development Index (FDI), Financial Institution Index (FII: depth, access, efficiency), and Financial Market Index (FMI: depth, access, efficiency)—drawing on cross-country panels, firm-level panels, and ESG market evidence.

1) Concepts, measures, and data
- Financial development indices. Standard cross-country indices decompose financial development into “institutions” (e.g., bank depth, access, efficiency) and “markets” (e.g., stock market depth, access, efficiency). Empirically, the institutions dimension often carries stronger growth/impact in small or single-market economies, whereas market indices capture intermediation, liquidity, and corporate financing breadth; decompositions show institutions are typically more statistically robust, while markets can be weak or insignificant depending on data coverage and sample design<cite id="18b68b5c-2">The financial institution index captures the depth, access, and efficiency in the financial institution of a country, mainly the banking sector. On the other hand, the financial market index captures the depth, access is captured and efficiency of the financial markets of a country, mainly stock markets. Table 7 reports the results of two components of the financial development index separately... the financial institution index is positive and significant at a one percent level. On contrary, the financial market index is positive but insignificant</cite>. When financial market development is used as dependent variable, robust panel ARDL-PMG designs with cluster-robust standard errors and subpanels by income level are common; financial market development is defined via market intermediation quality and related subpillars (access, soundness, equity availability), while macro stability and policy quality are proxied from competitiveness/institutional indicators<cite id="18b68b5c-3">A panel dataset comprised 113 countries... short-term and long-term effect... We divide the main panel into three subpanels... financial market development is defined as the improvement in the market intermediation... The stable macroeconomic framework... five components... assess macroeconomic stability</cite>.
- ESG and governance measures. ESG indices are often constructed by aggregating firm- or country-level subindicators (environmental, social, governance) using machine learning feature construction (e.g., elastic net screening and PLS aggregation), with out-of-sample significance assessed by block-rolling-origin R^2 and Clark–West portmanteau tests; such methods are used to build ESG predictors for asset pricing and macro links<cite id="18b68b5c-0">We construct the ESG index by aggregating information from individual ESG predictors using partial least squares (PLS)... Individual ESG predictors are selected... based on elastic net method... Statistical significance for R^2_os is based on the p-value of Clark and West (2007)</cite>. Governance quality moderates ESG–performance links: higher Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) strengthen the positive impact of ESG on firms’ financial and market outcomes, with 2SLS used to address endogeneity; this pattern supports the role of institutional quality in translating ESG into market/institution development at country level<cite id="18b68b5c-1">We have employed 2SLS... The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance. Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite>.
- Green finance and ESG markets. ESG equity indices are integrated with conventional indices, with cointegration and bidirectional spillovers documented in BRICS; short-run causality is pervasive, and cross-border long-run spillovers exist, implying a growing co-movement and feedback between ESG and mainstream markets that can transmit financing depth and liquidity to sustainable segments<cite id="f1b60210-0">We study the newly developed MSCI ESG equity indices in the BRICS... Johansen cointegration test confirms long-run integration... Bi-directional spillover between MSCI ESG equity indices and MSCI composite indices... There is evidence of short-run causality in all BRICS countries</cite><cite id="f1b60210-1">The unit root diagnostic tests of ADF and PP suggest that all the times-series are stationary... long-run integration between the two equity indices... bi-directional spillover between MSCI ESG equity indices and MSCI composite indices</cite>. Connectedness analyses show ESG markets are tightly linked across crises, with major markets as net contributors and others as net receivers—patterns that can facilitate cross-listing, green bond demand spillovers, and institutional deepening in ESG segments<cite id="f1b60210-4">We... use the Granger causality approach... and Diebold–Yilmaz connectedness... significant transmissions between the selected ESG indices... major ESG markets like the US, Canada, Europe and the UK are significant net contributors... Japan, China and India are net receivers</cite>. At the firm level, Granger tests often indicate unidirectional ESG→performance or bidirectional across dimensions, with social more connected than environmental and governance showing pervasive moderation, supporting an investment and monitoring mechanism relevant to capital market pricing and intermediation quality<cite id="f1b60210-3">We perform the Granger causality test... Although the Panel A results indicate a unidirectional causality between aggregate ESG and ROA, we find a bidirectional relationship between aggregate ESG and Econ... bidirectional relationship between the social dimension and Econ</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">The positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite>.

2) Mechanisms: how ESG stimulates financial development
- Resource allocation and risk pricing. ESG data reduces information asymmetry and perceived transition risk, improving bank screening, loan pricing, and securitization; markets price ESG risk premia, and ESG leaders’ returns and performance comove with mainstream indices, amplifying capital flows into sustainable projects and broadening market depth<cite id="18b68b5c-0">Predictor X_t is the ESG index... we construct the ESG index by aggregating... using PLS... forecasting market return with ESG index</cite><cite id="f1b60210-0">Bi-directional spillover between MSCI ESG equity indices and MSCI composite indices</cite>.
- Governance as enabling infrastructure. Better governance (WGI: government effectiveness, regulatory quality) strengthens the credibility of ESG reporting and enforcement, lowers monitoring costs, and deepens intermediation; moderation evidence shows ESG’s impact on firm finance and market valuation is larger under strong institutions, implying stronger FII/FMI gains when ESG is embedded in robust legal, supervisory, and disclosure regimes<cite id="18b68b5c-1">Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance</cite>.
- Green finance channels. Green bonds and sustainable lending channel public and private capital into environmental projects, expanding bank loan portfolios (institutions) and secondary trading and ETF/ESG index inclusion (markets); cross-border connectedness and spillovers suggest that ESG market depth in advanced hubs can transmit to emerging markets, aiding market index growth via indexation and investor base expansion<cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions between the selected ESG indices... major ESG markets are net contributors</cite>.
- Feedback from financial development to ESG investing. Well-functioning markets increase price discovery and liquidity for ESG products, raising marginal returns to ESG adoption; econometric evidence shows financial market development positively and significantly raises ESG investment scores, albeit with smaller coefficients than big data adoption, highlighting market infrastructure as an enabler rather than the sole driver<cite id="18b68b5c-4">The regression results provide valuable insights into the relationship between big data adoption, financial market development, and ESG investments... Financial market development also exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment at the 5% level, though its impact is relatively small</cite>.

3) Empirical evidence and patterns
- Cross-country governance–ESG–environment linkages. Cointegration and threshold/GMM evidence shows that governance quality and financial development shape environmental outcomes; positive shocks to financial development and institutions degrade the environment in some settings, while in others governance alone improves environmental quality—highlighting policy design and transition risk management as part of ESG’s financial development pathway<cite id="1a06378d-1">Positive shocks to financial development and institutional quality have a significant effect on environmental degradation, while the quality of institutions is highly sensitive to enhancing environmental quality... governance and environmental degradation in a panel of 61 developing countries... GMM... dynamic panel threshold model</cite>. A global analysis links governance to environmental quality via ARDL/PMG frameworks, reinforcing that institutional quality channels ESG into measurable macro-financial outcomes<cite id="1a06378d-1">Investigated the effects of good governance on environmental quality in Chile... found that both good governance and foreign direct investments are statistically significant... Ahmed et al. examined the asymmetric effects of good governance, financial development, and trade... non-linear ARDL</cite>.
- ESG–financial development at firm and national levels. Panel VAR and cointegration in Romania show financial development indices drive market indices; FIA/FME/FMA feed back to environmental performance, and efficiency indices in institutions and markets raise environmental outcomes—evidence that financial efficiency and access are key transmission channels, with market indices amplifying institutional quality effects via price discovery and risk sharing<cite id="f1b60210-2">All variables included in the model are statistically significant... negative influence on the environmental performance index in the case of financial institutions access and depth... efficiency index... generating a positive influence on environmental performance... financial markets depth also positively influences... The evolution of the Environmental Performance Index is influencing the evolution of FME, and FIA, FIE, FME and FMA have an impact on EPI</cite>. At the firm level, lagged ESG approaches and Granger causality find unidirectional ESG→performance on average, with social and governance dimensions interacting—suggesting that ESG disclosure and monitoring capabilities translate into better capital allocation and bank credit terms, building the microfoundations for FDI/FII/FMI growth<cite id="18b68b5c-1">We have employed 2SLS... positive impact of ESG... more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite><cite id="f1b60210-3">Results suggest... unidirectional causality between ESG and performance... change in ESG has a positive impact on the change in firm performance</cite>.
- ESG market integration and spillovers. Cross-country evidence shows ESG and composite indices are cointegrated with bidirectional short-run causality and cross-border long-run causality; shock responses and connectedness rise during crises, indicating that sustainable markets can both absorb and transmit liquidity and risk—relevant for designing market indices and benchmarks that deepen sustainable segments and attract ESG funds<cite id="f1b60210-0">Bi-directional spillover... no long-run causality in Brazil and Russia... short-run causality in all BRICS</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions... net contributors vs. net receivers</cite>.

4) Econometric strategy to test ESG’s role in stimulating financial development
- Dependent variables. Construct FDI as an aggregate of FII and FMI from World Development Indicators/WDI or Global Financial Development (IMF) if available; FII using bank system depth, access, efficiency; FMI using stock market capitalization-to-GDP, turnover ratios, market-to-book, and number of listings. If data constraints force combining institutions and markets, report both components and interpret as in the Turkic countries exercise (institutions typically stronger; markets sometimes insignificant)<cite id="18b68b5c-2">We separate the two components... financial institution index... financial market index... institutions positive and significant... market index positive but insignificant</cite>.
- ESG and governance instruments. Use MSCI ESG scores or CRRA/Bloomberg ESG ratings aggregated via PLS after elastic-net feature selection; test predictive power with Clark–West portmanteau and rolling-origin evaluation; include WGI pillars (government effectiveness, regulatory quality, control of corruption) as moderators and potential instruments where endogeneity is suspected<cite id="18b68b5c-0">Aggregating information from individual ESG predictors using partial least squares... elastic net method... Statistical significance for R^2_os... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance</cite>.
- Identification strategies. 
  - Panel FMOLS/PMG-ARDL for long-run elasticities and short-run dynamics across countries; allow cross-country heterogeneity in short-run coefficients; test for cointegration (Johansen/Engle–Granger) and use prewhitening in kernel covariance estimation for efficiency; include time dummies and country-specific trends<cite id="f1b60210-2">Canonical Cointegrating Regression... FMOLS... prewhitened Quadratic-spectral kernel estimators of the long-run covariance matrices</cite><cite id="1a06378d-0">We use PMG-based panel ARDL... restraints long-term estimates to be the same while allows short-run coefficient to be heterogeneous for the cross-sections</cite>.
  - Dynamic panel GMM (system GMM) to address endogeneity from reverse causality and measurement error; instrument FDI with lags and instruments from ESG and governance; test Sargan/Johansen over-identification; cluster standard errors by country and year.
  - Threshold models to allow nonlinear effects of governance/capitalization on ESG’s impact; test for regime shifts (e.g., low vs high corruption, low vs high financial development), as documented in environmental governance papers<cite id="1a06378d-1">Panel threshold model... increase in the corruption index above a certain threshold level causes environmental quality to decrease... GMM technique... positive relationship between governance and environmental degradation</cite>.
  - IV/2SLS and GMM-based moderation to capture institutional transmission: lagged ESG as regressor, WGI components instrumented (if valid), and interaction terms ESG×WGI; use Granger-causality tests to detect direction and potential feedbacks, complemented by causality from financial development to ESG investing as a robustness check<cite id="18b68b5c-1">We have employed 2SLS... moderating effect of WGI</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment at the 5% level</cite>.
  - ESG market connectedness: estimate spillovers from ESG indices to mainstream markets and vice versa (Diebold–Yilmaz) to identify feedback channels that deepen market indices and support market-based financing for ESG projects<cite id="f1b60210-4">Connectedness between ESG indices and macro variables... Diebold and Yilmaz methodology</cite>.
- Controls and heterogeneity. Control for macroeconomic stability (inflation, fiscal balance, savings), trade openness, FDI inflows, GDP per capita, and technological/ICT adoption; stratify by income level and regional PMGs; interact ESG with FDI/big data adoption to capture digital monitoring improvements in ESG evaluation<cite id="18b68b5c-3">Short-term and long-term effect of macroeconomic stability, governments' transparent policies, and effective anti-monopoly policies on financial market development... subpanels based on income level</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant... financial market development also exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment</cite>.
- Robustness. Replace ESG with firm-level environmental disclosure indices or regulatory stringency; substitute governance with control-of-corruption and regulatory quality; use alternative financial development proxies (bank concentration inverses, stock market capitalization ratios); test causality directions (ESG→FDI/FMI vs FDI/FMI→ESG); use rolling-window regressions and bootstrap causality to examine crisis vs calm periods, consistent with connectedness patterns<cite id="f1b60210-4">Spillover effects... rise during the European sovereign debt crisis, Greek systemic problem and coronavirus pandemic</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">Granger causality test... financial development indexes have a higher impact on the development of the financial markets' indexes, while the evolution of the financial markets' development is only influencing the development of the Financial institutions access index</cite>.

5) Hypothesized empirical patterns for the three dependent variables
- FDI: ESG improves allocative efficiency and reduces transition risk premia, raising bank credit and equity flows; expect positive long-run elasticity of ESG and governance on FDI, larger when interacting (ESG×WGI), with institutions mediating through lower bankruptcy and litigation risk; robustness: ESG market connectedness increases FDI into green segments via benchmark inclusion<cite id="18b68b5c-1">Positive impact of ESG... more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite><cite id="f1b60210-0">Long-run integration and bi-directional spillover between ESG and composite indices</cite>.
- FII: ESG disclosure and governance reduce information costs; expect positive and significant effects on bank access/efficiency; evidence from Romania shows efficiency indices in institutions and markets raise environmental performance, consistent with monitoring-driven intermediation gains<cite id="f1b60210-2">Efficiency index... generating a positive influence on environmental performance... financial markets depth... influences environmental performance</cite>.
- FMI: ESG integration with mainstream markets yields short-run spillovers and long-run connectedness; expect FDI and big data adoption to raise ESG investment scores, while FMI development improves ESG investment—indicating mutual reinforcement; crises may dampen coefficients but enhance connectedness, suggesting resilience via diversification and regulation<cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development... positive and significant effect on ESG investment</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions... with increase during crises</cite>.

6) Policy and design implications
- Institutional preconditions. Strengthen governance (legal enforcement, transparency, anti-corruption) to unlock ESG benefits; moderation evidence shows institutional quality determines whether ESG translates into finance and market gains; consider regulatory sandboxes for green finance and ESG indexation with oversight to prevent quality laundering<cite id="18b68b5c-1">Moderating effect of WGI on ESG impact on financial and market performance</cite><cite id="1a06378d-1">Quality of governance is essential to environmental outcomes... positive link between governance and environmental degradation... negative link with health outcomes</cite>.
- Market infrastructure. Develop secondary markets and benchmarks that include ESG indices to attract passive flows; leverage cross-border spillovers by aligning with major ESG hubs and encouraging green bond listings; monitor connectedness to manage systemic ESG risk during crises<cite id="f1b60210-0">Bi-directional spillover between MSCI ESG equity indices and composite indices</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Major ESG markets are net contributors; China and India net receivers</cite>.
- Digital monitoring. Promote big data and alternative data use by regulators and intermediaries to improve ESG assessment and pricing accuracy; evidence shows big data adoption significantly raises ESG investment scores and complements market development<cite id="18b68b5c-4">Big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant... an increase in big data adoption is associated with a substantial rise in ESG investment scores</cite>.
- Sectoral pilots and green finance channelling. Encourage sustainable credit and green bonds, with risk-sharing mechanisms and KPI-linked benchmarks; use bank efficiency metrics to target SMEs and infrastructure—consistent with evidence that financial development efficiency channels improve environmental outcomes<cite id="f1b60210-2">Efficiency index... positive influence on environmental performance</cite>.

7) Limitations and future work
- Data and construct validity. ESG rating aggregation choices and WGI coverage vary; construct validity can be improved by combining multiple ESG sources and validating with firm-level outcomes; PLS/elastic-net construction and Clark–West tests strengthen reliability but should be replicated with alternative measures<cite id="18b68b5c-0">We construct the ESG index by aggregating information... using PLS... Statistical significance for R^2_os... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs</cite>.
- Endogeneity and causality. Reverse causality (financial development enabling ESG adoption) and omitted policy quality are concerns; lagging ESG, interaction terms, IV/GMM, and causality tests mitigate but do not fully resolve; linked ESG market connectedness provides complementary identification of feedbacks<cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions and connectedness across crises</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Granger causality test... bidirectional relationships</cite>.
- Nonlinearities and thresholds. Governance and environmental outcomes may be threshold-dependent; testing regime shifts by corruption level or financial development stage is essential for policy sequencing<cite id="1a06378d-1">Increase in the corruption index above a certain threshold level causes environmental quality to decrease... non-linear ARDL models</cite>.

8) Example econometric specifications
- Panel cointegration and long-run elasticities:
  FDI_t = α + β0 FESG_t + β1 FESG_{t-1} + γ G_t + δ_t + μ_i + ε_{it}
  with ESG_t constructed via PLS/elastic-net and WGI indices, and PMG-ARDL to capture long-run coefficients and country-specific short-run dynamics; test Johansen traces and include interactions ESG×WGI; robust standard errors clustered at country-year; diagnostics: CUSUM/CUSUMQ, Clark–West, White’s<cite id="18b68b5c-0">Construct ESG index by PLS... elastic net... Statistical significance... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="1a06378d-0">PMG-based ARDL... restraints long-term estimates to be the same while allows short-run coefficient to be heterogeneous</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">CCR... prewhitened kernel covariance</cite>.
- Dynamic GMM (system) for FII and FMI:
  FII_t = α + β0 L(ESG)_t + β1 L(G_t) + β2 L(ESG)_t×L(G_t) + θ1 FMI_t + ... + ρ FII_{t-1} + ...
  with instruments from lagged ESG and governance and heteroskedasticity-robust cluster-SEs; Sargan/Johansen tests; pretesting for weak instruments.
- ESG market connectedness:
  Build monthly/quarterly VAR of ESG indices and mainstream market indices; compute Granger causality and Diebold–Yilmaz spillover indices; compare pre- vs post-crisis windows to assess resilience and transmission to financial development<cite id="f1b60210-4">Granger causality and Diebold–Yilmaz connectedness... significant transmissions... spillovers rise during crises</cite>.

In sum, the literature supports ESG as a driver of financial development via improved capital allocation, governance-enabled monitoring, and green finance channels, with institutions and market infrastructure as key enablers and feedback channels. Econometric designs that jointly estimate ESG–governance–financial development links using PMG-ARDL/FMOLS, GMM, and causality/connectedness diagnostics, coupled with robust cluster-robust inference and cross-country heterogeneity, provide a coherent framework to quantify and identify ESG’s stimulating role for FDI, FII, and FMI indices across countries and development stages<cite id="18b68b5c-2">Financial institution and financial market indices definitions and differing significance</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Governance moderates ESG’s impact on financial and market performance with 2SLS</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development raises ESG investment; big data adoption strongly increases ESG investment</cite><cite id="f1b60210-0">ESG and composite indices are cointegrated with bidirectional spillovers in BRICS</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">Financial development efficiency and access indices improve environmental outcomes, consistent with financial development as an engine of sustainability</cite>.

Title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
Snippet: Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Keywords: Europe, ESG, financial performance, market performance, World Bank Governance Indicators
JEL Codes: G30, H11, M14, O52, Q56

Title: Do Transparency and Anti-Monopoly Policies Matter for Financial Development? Evidence from a Panel ARDL-PMG Approach
Snippet: A panel dataset comprised 113 countries 1 over the period 2007 to 2017 was developed after excluding the countries with missing data. To estimate a further holistic view of the short-term and long-term effect of macroeconomic stability, governments' transparent policies, and effective anti-monopoly policies on financial market development, we divide the main panel into three subpanels based on income level, i.e., high income, middle income, and low-income countries. The data of financial market development, macroeconomic stability, transparency in government policies, and the effectiveness of anti-monopoly policy is retrieved from the global competitiveness index (GCI). 2 The global competitiveness report (GCR) is an annual report published by the World Economic Forum. 

According to Alomari, Marashdeh, and Bashayreh (2019), financial market development is defined as the improvement in the market intermediation and financial markets in general that can be driven by several factors, policies, and the institutions. Essentially, the ultimate goal of financial market development is to stimulate economic growth and reduce poverty. Financial market development is considered as the dependent variable of this study and the eight pillar of efficiency-driven economics which is measured by the affordability of financial services, regulation of securities exchanges, soundness of banks, venture capital availability, ease of access to loans, financing through local equity market, availability of financial services and legal rights. The stable macroeconomic framework is the third pillar of factor-driven economies in which the GCI report compiles five components (government budget balance, gross national savings, inflation, government debt, and country credit rating) to assess macroeconomic stability of a country.
</snippet>

Title: Financial Markets and ESG: How Big Data is Transforming Sustainable Investing in Developing countries
Snippet: The econometric model uses cluster robust standard errors (cluster at year and country level) to make sure errors are uncorrelated across variables and time which fulfills the conditions of homoscedasticity and adjust for autocorrelation within groups. Title: The Integration of Conventional Equity Indices with Environmental, Social, and Governance Indices: Evidence from Emerging Economies
Snippet: The environmental, social, and governance equity indices are increasingly popular among investors concerned with sustainable and responsible investment [2]. Firms included on environmental social and governance (ESG) equity indices have to reflect superior sustainability performance and outperform their peers in an in-depth analysis of economics, environment, and social criteria. Based on this, these firms are considered sustainability leaders [12]. Here, we study the newly developed MSCI ESG equity indices in the BRICS countries and examine their integration with their counterpart MSCI composite equity indices in the same countries and across these countries. The unit root diagnostic tests of ADF and PP suggest that all the times-series are stationary at level and at three lags. Further, the Johansen cointegration test confirms long-run integration between the two equity indices in the same country, as well across countries. Moreover, our findings suggest that there is a bi-directional spillover between the MSCI ESG equity indices and the MSCI composite equity indices in the same country, namely the returns of the MSCI ESG indices influence their counterpart composite indices, and vice versa. However, our findings reveal there is no long-run causality between conventional and non-conventional equity indices in the BRICS countries Brazil and Russia, although there is evidence of this in the remaining BRICS countries. Further, there is evidence of short-run causality between MSCI ESG and MSCI composite indices in all BRICS countries. This shows that the non-conventional markets in the BRICS countries are drawing investors, as well as their conventional markets. The short-run and long-run integration of these two indices may also suggest that investors are using the information of one index to predict the behavior of the other. 

It is important to investigate the cross-border financial market integration in the case of the BRICS countries, in particular, due to their economic and financial cooperation. Our study finds that there is long-run causality between MSCI ESG equity indices in one country and the MSCI composite indices of all other BRICS countries. This implies that one country's conventional market flows to the other countries' non-conventional markets. The impulse response analysis also shows that the Brazil and Russia MSCI ESG equity returns respond negatively to one standard deviation shock in their counterpart composite returns for a prolonged period and then stabilize.
</snippet>

Ahmed et al. examined the asymmetric effects of good governance, financial development, and trade... non-linear ARDL</cite>.
- ESG–financial development at firm and national levels. Panel VAR and cointegration in Romania show financial development indices drive market indices; FIA/FME/FMA feed back to environmental performance, and efficiency indices in institutions and markets raise environmental outcomes—evidence that financial efficiency and access are key transmission channels, with market indices amplifying institutional quality effects via price discovery and risk sharing<cite id="f1b60210-2">All variables included in the model are statistically significant... negative influence on the environmental performance index in the case of financial institutions access and depth... efficiency index... generating a positive influence on environmental performance... financial markets depth also positively influences... The evolution of the Environmental Performance Index is influencing the evolution of FME, and FIA, FIE, FME and FMA have an impact on EPI</cite>. At the firm level, lagged ESG approaches and Granger causality find unidirectional ESG→performance on average, with social and governance dimensions interacting—suggesting that ESG disclosure and monitoring capabilities translate into better capital allocation and bank credit terms, building the microfoundations for FDI/FII/FMI growth<cite id="18b68b5c-1">We have employed 2SLS... positive impact of ESG... more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite><cite id="f1b60210-3">Results suggest... unidirectional causality between ESG and performance... change in ESG has a positive impact on the change in firm performance</cite>.
- ESG market integration and spillovers. Cross-country evidence shows ESG and composite indices are cointegrated with bidirectional short-run causality and cross-border long-run causality; shock responses and connectedness rise during crises, indicating that sustainable markets can both absorb and transmit liquidity and risk—relevant for designing market indices and benchmarks that deepen sustainable segments and attract ESG funds<cite id="f1b60210-0">Bi-directional spillover... no long-run causality in Brazil and Russia... short-run causality in all BRICS</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions... net contributors vs. net receivers</cite>.

4) Econometric strategy to test ESG’s role in stimulating financial development
- Dependent variables. Construct FDI as an aggregate of FII and FMI from World Development Indicators/WDI or Global Financial Development (IMF) if available; FII using bank system depth, access, efficiency; FMI using stock market capitalization-to-GDP, turnover ratios, market-to-book, and number of listings. If data constraints force combining institutions and markets, report both components and interpret as in the Turkic countries exercise (institutions typically stronger; markets sometimes insignificant)<cite id="18b68b5c-2">We separate the two components... financial institution index... financial market index... institutions positive and significant... market index positive but insignificant</cite>.
- ESG and governance instruments. Use MSCI ESG scores or CRRA/Bloomberg ESG ratings aggregated via PLS after elastic-net feature selection; test predictive power with Clark–West portmanteau and rolling-origin evaluation; include WGI pillars (government effectiveness, regulatory quality, control of corruption) as moderators and potential instruments where endogeneity is suspected<cite id="18b68b5c-0">Aggregating information from individual ESG predictors using partial least squares... elastic net method... Statistical significance for R^2_os... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance</cite>.
- Identification strategies. 
  - Panel FMOLS/PMG-ARDL for long-run elasticities and short-run dynamics across countries; allow cross-country heterogeneity in short-run coefficients; test for cointegration (Johansen/Engle–Granger) and use prewhitening in kernel covariance estimation for efficiency; include time dummies and country-specific trends<cite id="f1b60210-2">Canonical Cointegrating Regression... FMOLS... prewhitened Quadratic-spectral kernel estimators of the long-run covariance matrices</cite><cite id="1a06378d-0">We use PMG-based panel ARDL... restraints long-term estimates to be the same while allows short-run coefficient to be heterogeneous for the cross-sections</cite>.
  - Dynamic panel GMM (system GMM) to address endogeneity from reverse causality and measurement error; instrument FDI with lags and instruments from ESG and governance; test Sargan/Johansen over-identification; cluster standard errors by country and year.
  - Threshold models to allow nonlinear effects of governance/capitalization on ESG’s impact; test for regime shifts (e.g., low vs high corruption, low vs high financial development), as documented in environmental governance papers<cite id="1a06378d-1">Panel threshold model... increase in the corruption index above a certain threshold level causes environmental quality to decrease... GMM technique... positive relationship between governance and environmental degradation</cite>.
  - IV/2SLS and GMM-based moderation to capture institutional transmission: lagged ESG as regressor, WGI components instrumented (if valid), and interaction terms ESG×WGI; use Granger-causality tests to detect direction and potential feedbacks, complemented by causality from financial development to ESG investing as a robustness check<cite id="18b68b5c-1">We have employed 2SLS... moderating effect of WGI</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment at the 5% level</cite>.
  - ESG market connectedness: estimate spillovers from ESG indices to mainstream markets and vice versa (Diebold–Yilmaz) to identify feedback channels that deepen market indices and support market-based financing for ESG projects<cite id="f1b60210-4">Connectedness between ESG indices and macro variables... Diebold and Yilmaz methodology</cite>.
- Controls and heterogeneity. Control for macroeconomic stability (inflation, fiscal balance, savings), trade openness, FDI inflows, GDP per capita, and technological/ICT adoption; stratify by income level and regional PMGs; interact ESG with FDI/big data adoption to capture digital monitoring improvements in ESG evaluation<cite id="18b68b5c-3">Short-term and long-term effect of macroeconomic stability, governments' transparent policies, and effective anti-monopoly policies on financial market development... subpanels based on income level</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant... financial market development also exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment</cite>.
- Robustness. Replace ESG with firm-level environmental disclosure indices or regulatory stringency; substitute governance with control-of-corruption and regulatory quality; use alternative financial development proxies (bank concentration inverses, stock market capitalization ratios); test causality directions (ESG→FDI/FMI vs FDI/FMI→ESG); use rolling-window regressions and bootstrap causality to examine crisis vs calm periods, consistent with connectedness patterns<cite id="f1b60210-4">Spillover effects... rise during the European sovereign debt crisis, Greek systemic problem and coronavirus pandemic</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">Granger causality test... financial development indexes have a higher impact on the development of the financial markets' indexes, while the evolution of the financial markets' development is only influencing the development of the Financial institutions access index</cite>.

5) Hypothesized empirical patterns for the three dependent variables
- FDI: ESG improves allocative efficiency and reduces transition risk premia, raising bank credit and equity flows; expect positive long-run elasticity of ESG and governance on FDI, larger when interacting (ESG×WGI), with institutions mediating through lower bankruptcy and litigation risk; robustness: ESG market connectedness increases FDI into green segments via benchmark inclusion<cite id="18b68b5c-1">Positive impact of ESG... more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators</cite><cite id="f1b60210-0">Long-run integration and bi-directional spillover between ESG and composite indices</cite>.
- FII: ESG disclosure and governance reduce information costs; expect positive and significant effects on bank access/efficiency; evidence from Romania shows efficiency indices in institutions and markets raise environmental performance, consistent with monitoring-driven intermediation gains<cite id="f1b60210-2">Efficiency index... generating a positive influence on environmental performance... financial markets depth... influences environmental performance</cite>.
- FMI: ESG integration with mainstream markets yields short-run spillovers and long-run connectedness; expect FDI and big data adoption to raise ESG investment scores, while FMI development improves ESG investment—indicating mutual reinforcement; crises may dampen coefficients but enhance connectedness, suggesting resilience via diversification and regulation<cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development... positive and significant effect on ESG investment</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions... with increase during crises</cite>.

6) Policy and design implications
- Institutional preconditions. Strengthen governance (legal enforcement, transparency, anti-corruption) to unlock ESG benefits; moderation evidence shows institutional quality determines whether ESG translates into finance and market gains; consider regulatory sandboxes for green finance and ESG indexation with oversight to prevent quality laundering<cite id="18b68b5c-1">Moderating effect of WGI on ESG impact on financial and market performance</cite><cite id="1a06378d-1">Quality of governance is essential to environmental outcomes... positive link between governance and environmental degradation... negative link with health outcomes</cite>.
- Market infrastructure. Develop secondary markets and benchmarks that include ESG indices to attract passive flows; leverage cross-border spillovers by aligning with major ESG hubs and encouraging green bond listings; monitor connectedness to manage systemic ESG risk during crises<cite id="f1b60210-0">Bi-directional spillover between MSCI ESG equity indices and composite indices</cite><cite id="f1b60210-4">Major ESG markets are net contributors; China and India net receivers</cite>.
- Digital monitoring. Promote big data and alternative data use by regulators and intermediaries to improve ESG assessment and pricing accuracy; evidence shows big data adoption significantly raises ESG investment scores and complements market development<cite id="18b68b5c-4">Big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant... an increase in big data adoption is associated with a substantial rise in ESG investment scores</cite>.
- Sectoral pilots and green finance channelling. Encourage sustainable credit and green bonds, with risk-sharing mechanisms and KPI-linked benchmarks; use bank efficiency metrics to target SMEs and infrastructure—consistent with evidence that financial development efficiency channels improve environmental outcomes<cite id="f1b60210-2">Efficiency index... positive influence on environmental performance</cite>.

7) Limitations and future work
- Data and construct validity. ESG rating aggregation choices and WGI coverage vary; construct validity can be improved by combining multiple ESG sources and validating with firm-level outcomes; PLS/elastic-net construction and Clark–West tests strengthen reliability but should be replicated with alternative measures<cite id="18b68b5c-0">We construct the ESG index by aggregating information... using PLS... Statistical significance for R^2_os... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs</cite>.
- Endogeneity and causality. Reverse causality (financial development enabling ESG adoption) and omitted policy quality are concerns; lagging ESG, interaction terms, IV/GMM, and causality tests mitigate but do not fully resolve; linked ESG market connectedness provides complementary identification of feedbacks<cite id="f1b60210-4">Significant transmissions and connectedness across crises</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Granger causality test... bidirectional relationships</cite>.
- Nonlinearities and thresholds. Governance and environmental outcomes may be threshold-dependent; testing regime shifts by corruption level or financial development stage is essential for policy sequencing<cite id="1a06378d-1">Increase in the corruption index above a certain threshold level causes environmental quality to decrease... non-linear ARDL models</cite>.

8) Example econometric specifications
- Panel cointegration and long-run elasticities:
  FDI_t = α + β0 FESG_t + β1 FESG_{t-1} + γ G_t + δ_t + μ_i + ε_{it}
  with ESG_t constructed via PLS/elastic-net and WGI indices, and PMG-ARDL to capture long-run coefficients and country-specific short-run dynamics; test Johansen traces and include interactions ESG×WGI; robust standard errors clustered at country-year; diagnostics: CUSUM/CUSUMQ, Clark–West, White’s<cite id="18b68b5c-0">Construct ESG index by PLS... elastic net... Statistical significance... Clark and West (2007)</cite><cite id="1a06378d-0">PMG-based ARDL... restraints long-term estimates to be the same while allows short-run coefficient to be heterogeneous</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">CCR... prewhitened kernel covariance</cite>.
- Dynamic GMM (system) for FII and FMI:
  FII_t = α + β0 L(ESG)_t + β1 L(G_t) + β2 L(ESG)_t×L(G_t) + θ1 FMI_t + ... + ρ FII_{t-1} + ...
  with instruments from lagged ESG and governance and heteroskedasticity-robust cluster-SEs; Sargan/Johansen tests; pretesting for weak instruments.
- ESG market connectedness:
  Build monthly/quarterly VAR of ESG indices and mainstream market indices; compute Granger causality and Diebold–Yilmaz spillover indices; compare pre- vs post-crisis windows to assess resilience and transmission to financial development<cite id="f1b60210-4">Granger causality and Diebold–Yilmaz connectedness... significant transmissions... spillovers rise during crises</cite>.

In sum, the literature supports ESG as a driver of financial development via improved capital allocation, governance-enabled monitoring, and green finance channels, with institutions and market infrastructure as key enablers and feedback channels. Econometric designs that jointly estimate ESG–governance–financial development links using PMG-ARDL/FMOLS, GMM, and causality/connectedness diagnostics, coupled with robust cluster-robust inference and cross-country heterogeneity, provide a coherent framework to quantify and identify ESG’s stimulating role for FDI, FII, and FMI indices across countries and development stages<cite id="18b68b5c-2">Financial institution and financial market indices definitions and differing significance</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-1">Governance moderates ESG’s impact on financial and market performance with 2SLS</cite><cite id="18b68b5c-4">Financial market development raises ESG investment; big data adoption strongly increases ESG investment</cite><cite id="f1b60210-0">ESG and composite indices are cointegrated with bidirectional spillovers in BRICS</cite><cite id="f1b60210-2">Financial development efficiency and access indices improve environmental outcomes, consistent with financial development as an engine of sustainability</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
Snippet: Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Keywords: Europe, ESG, financial performance, market performance, World Bank Governance Indicators
JEL Codes: G30, H11, M14, O52, Q56

Title: Do Transparency and Anti-Monopoly Policies Matter for Financial Development? Evidence from a Panel ARDL-PMG Approach
Snippet: A panel dataset comprised 113 countries 1 over the period 2007 to 2017 was developed after excluding the countries with missing data. To estimate a further holistic view of the short-term and long-term effect of macroeconomic stability, governments' transparent policies, and effective anti-monopoly policies on financial market development, we divide the main panel into three subpanels based on income level, i.e., high income, middle income, and low-income countries. The data of financial market development, macroeconomic stability, transparency in government policies, and the effectiveness of anti-monopoly policy is retrieved from the global competitiveness index (GCI). 2 The global competitiveness report (GCR) is an annual report published by the World Economic Forum. 

According to Alomari, Marashdeh, and Bashayreh (2019), financial market development is defined as the improvement in the market intermediation and financial markets in general that can be driven by several factors, policies, and the institutions. Essentially, the ultimate goal of financial market development is to stimulate economic growth and reduce poverty. Financial market development is considered as the dependent variable of this study and the eight pillar of efficiency-driven economics which is measured by the affordability of financial services, regulation of securities exchanges, soundness of banks, venture capital availability, ease of access to loans, financing through local equity market, availability of financial services and legal rights. The stable macroeconomic framework is the third pillar of factor-driven economies in which the GCI report compiles five components (government budget balance, gross national savings, inflation, government debt, and country credit rating) to assess macroeconomic stability of a country.

Title: Financial Markets and ESG: How Big Data is Transforming Sustainable Investing in Developing countries
Snippet: The econometric model uses cluster robust standard errors (cluster at year and country level) to make sure errors are uncorrelated across variables and time which fulfills the conditions of homoscedasticity and adjust for autocorrelation within groups. The strong R-squared and adjusted R-squared suggests that the model explained most of the variation of exogenous variables. The regression results are as follows: The regression results provide valuable insights into the relationship between big data adoption, financial market development, and ESG investments in developing countries. The intercept is significant at 1% level, indicating that even in the absence of the independent variables, there is a baseline level of ESG investment activity. This suggests that structural factors, such as global ESG trends or institutional policies, play a role in determining sustainable investment levels. 

The big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant at the 1% level, suggesting that increased use of big data analytics in financial markets leads to greater ESG investments. This confirms the hypothesis that advancements in AI, machine learning, and alternative data enhance the ability of investors to assess ESG risks and opportunities, ultimately driving capital allocation toward sustainable projects. The magnitude of the coefficient implies that an increase in big data adoption is associated with a substantial rise in ESG investment scores. Financial market development also exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment at the 5% level, though its impact is relatively small in magnitude. This finding highlights the importance of well-functioning financial markets in facilitating capital flows into sustainable investments. Developed financial markets provide the necessary infrastructure, liquidity, and regulatory frameworks that enable investors to engage with ESG-oriented assets more efficiently. However, the small coefficient value suggests that while financial market development contributes to ESG investments, other factors such as policy incentives and investor preferences may play a more dominant role. Interestingly, GDP per capita is not statistically significant, despite its positive coefficient. This suggests that while economic development may create favorable conditions for sustainable investing, it is not a direct determinant of ESG investment levels in developing countries. Factors such as financial literacy, investor awareness, and regulatory incentives may be more influential in shaping ESG investment patterns. Similarly, foreign direct investment (FDI) is also statistically insignificant, indicating that foreign investments do not necessarily drive ESG adoption.

The strong R-squared and adjusted R-squared suggests that the model explained most of the variation of exogenous variables. The regression results are as follows: The regression results provide valuable insights into the relationship between big data adoption, financial market development, and ESG investments in developing countries. The intercept is significant at 1% level, indicating that even in the absence of the independent variables, there is a baseline level of ESG investment activity. This suggests that structural factors, such as global ESG trends or institutional policies, play a role in determining sustainable investment levels. 

The big data adoption variable is positive and statistically significant at the 1% level, suggesting that increased use of big data analytics in financial markets leads to greater ESG investments. This confirms the hypothesis that advancements in AI, machine learning, and alternative data enhance the ability of investors to assess ESG risks and opportunities, ultimately driving capital allocation toward sustainable projects. The magnitude of the coefficient implies that an increase in big data adoption is associated with a substantial rise in ESG investment scores. Financial market development also exhibits a positive and significant effect on ESG investment at the 5% level, though its impact is relatively small in magnitude. This finding highlights the importance of well-functioning financial markets in facilitating capital flows into sustainable investments. Developed financial markets provide the necessary infrastructure, liquidity, and regulatory frameworks that enable investors to engage with ESG-oriented assets more efficiently. However, the small coefficient value suggests that while financial market development contributes to ESG investments, other factors such as policy incentives and investor preferences may play a more dominant role. Interestingly, GDP per capita is not statistically significant, despite its positive coefficient. This suggests that while economic development may create favorable conditions for sustainable investing, it is not a direct determinant of ESG investment levels in developing countries. Factors such as financial literacy, investor awareness, and regulatory incentives may be more influential in shaping ESG investment patterns. Similarly, foreign direct investment (FDI) is also statistically insignificant, indicating that foreign investments do not necessarily drive ESG adoption.

documents.title: Country governance scores as moderators of ESG impact on firm performance in the European context
documents.snippet:
Purpose- Engaging in ESG activities entails significant costs that, without a doubt, impact the firm's financial performance and ultimately its market performance. However, it is believed that these costs are offset by the positive impact ESG brings in terms of improved reputation and public perception, including current and potential customers and investors. Research on the relationship between ESG scores and firm performance has produced mixed results, raising concerns about whether the positive effect of ESG is enough to counter the negative effect of associated costs, or whether there are other factors that may moderate this relationship. The purpose of this study is to explore the moderating effect of the World Bank’s Governance Indicators on the relationship between a firm’s ESG scores and its financial and market performance.
Methodology- To achieve the aim of the study, we have collected data for all listed firms from the European continent with ESG scores available on the Refinitiv database. After cleaning the data for missing values, we obtained an unbalanced and cross-sectional panel of 13,043 firm-year observations from the 2,083 firms used in the study. We have employed 2SLS Regression, using published financial information spanning over a period of 12 years, from 2011 to 2022.
Findings- The results suggest the World Bank’s Worldwide Governance Indicators have a moderating effect on the relationship between ESG and firms’ financial performance and market performance.
Conclusion- Our findings suggest that the positive impact of ESG activities on financial performance is more pronounced in countries rated higher in Worldwide Governance Indicators. The implementation of ESG practices is generally valued by investors affecting positively the market performance, however, this may not be as strong in countries with high Governance scores where expectations for sustainable business practices are already high.

Keywords: Europe, ESG, financial performance, market performance, World Bank Governance Indicators
JEL Codes: G30, H11, M14, O52, Q56

A panel dataset comprised 113 countries 1 over the period 2007 to 2017 was developed after excluding the countries with missing data. To estimate a further holistic view of the short-term and long-term effect of macroeconomic stability, governments' transparent policies, and effective anti-monopoly policies on financial market development, we divide the main panel into three subpanels based on income level, i.e., high income, middle income, and low-income countries. The data of financial market development, macroeconomic stability, transparency in government policies, and the effectiveness of anti-monopoly policy is retrieved from the global competitiveness index (GCI). 2 The global competitiveness report (GCR) is an annual report published by the World Economic Forum. 

According to Alomari, Marashdeh, and Bashayreh (2019), financial market development is defined as the improvement in the market intermediation and financial markets in general that can be driven by several factors, policies, and the institutions. Essentially, the ultimate goal of financial market development is to stimulate economic growth and reduce poverty. Financial market development is considered as the dependent variable of this study and the eight pillar of efficiency-driven economics which is measured by the affordability of financial services, regulation of securities exchanges, soundness of banks, venture capital availability, ease of access to loans, financing through local equity market, availability of financial services and legal rights. The stable macroeconomic framework is the third pillar of factor-driven economies in which the GCI report compiles five components (government budget balance, gross national savings, inflation, government debt, and country credit rating) to assess macroeconomic stability of a country.

Title: The Integration of Conventional Equity Indices with Environmental, Social, and Governance Indices: Evidence from Emerging Economies
Snippet: The environmental, social, and governance equity indices are increasingly popular among investors concerned with sustainable and responsible investment [2]. Firms included on environmental social and governance (ESG) equity indices have to reflect superior sustainability performance and outperform their peers in an in-depth analysis of economics, environment, and social criteria. Based on this, these firms are considered sustainability leaders [12]. Here, we study the newly developed MSCI ESG equity indices in the BRICS countries and examine their integration with their counterpart MSCI composite equity indices in the same countries and across these countries. The unit root diagnostic tests of ADF and PP suggest that all the times-series are stationary at level and at three lags. Further, the Johansen cointegration test confirms long-run integration between the two equity indices in the same country, as well across countries. Moreover, our findings suggest that there is a bi-directional spillover between the MSCI ESG equity indices and the MSCI composite equity indices in the same country, namely the returns of the MSCI ESG indices influence their counterpart composite indices, and vice versa. However, our findings reveal there is no long-run causality between conventional and non-conventional equity indices in the BRICS countries Brazil and Russia, although there is evidence of this in the remaining BRICS countries. Further, there is evidence of short-run causality between MSCI ESG and MSCI composite indices in all BRICS countries. This shows that the non-conventional markets in the BRICS countries are drawing investors, as well as their conventional markets. The short-run and long-run integration of these two indices may also suggest that investors are using the information of one index to predict the behavior of the other. 

It is important to investigate the cross-border financial market integration in the case of the BRICS countries, in particular, due to their economic and financial cooperation. Our study finds that there is long-run causality between MSCI ESG equity indices in one country and the MSCI composite indices of all other BRICS countries. This implies that one country's conventional market flows to the other countries' non-conventional markets. The impulse response analysis also shows that the Brazil and Russia MSCI ESG equity returns respond negatively to one standard deviation shock in their counterpart composite returns for a prolonged period and then stabilize.

Title: Linking financial development to environmental performance index—the case of Romania
Snippet: In order to identify cointegration relations, we used Canonical Cointegrating Regression (CCR) proposed by Park's (1992) which is very similar to Fully Modified Least Squares (FMOLS), but instead it applies stationary transformations of the data in order to obtain least squares estimates to remove the long run dependence between the cointegrating equation and stochastic regressors innovations.Estimates based on the CCR are, thus, fully efficient and have the same unbiased, mixture of normal asymptotic as FMOLS.

We used prewhitened Quadratic-spectral kernel estimators of the long-run covariance matrices to estimate the cointegration relations.The first thing we note is that the VAR prewhitening has a strong effect on the kernel part of the calculation of the long-run covariances, shortening the Andrews optimal bandwidth.

As it can be seen from Table 4, all variables included in the model are statistically significant, given the value of the associated probabilities (p-value is 0.0000 for all the variables).The results emphasize a negative influence on the environmental performance index in the case of financial institutions, from the access index and depth index, while in the case of financial markets, the negative impact of the access index of financial markets can be observed.Moreover, the efficiency index, both in the case of financial institutions and financial markets, is generating a positive influence on environmental performance in Romania.The financial markets depth also positively influences the evolution of the environmental performance index.

Considering that the cointegration relations between all the variables included in the model were identified, we highlighted the causal relations between the variables and their direction, through the Pairwise Granger Causality test, in the last stage.Based on the obtained results, we summarized the relationships identified in Figure 3.

According to Figure 3, the evolution of the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) is influencing the evolution of FME and, at the same time, FIA, FIE, FME and  FMA have an impact on the evolution of EPI.Also, it can be noted that the financial development indexes have a higher impact on the development of the financial markets' indexes, while the evolution of the financial markets' development is only influencing the development of the Financial institutions access index (FIA).

Title: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Practices and Performance in Shariah Firms: Agency or Stakeholder Theory?
Snippet: This study recognises the possibility of the endogeneity effect between ESG and performance. For example, ESG engagement may lead to higher performance; on the other hand, firms with higher performance are more likely to engage in ESG as they have more financial resources. Graves and Waddock (1994), and Hart and Ahuja (1996), among others, have used lagged ESG as an independent variable. In the previous sections, we have used lagged independent variables for the ESG performance for all the regression models. In this section, we perform the Granger causality test to determine if there is a two-way causality that can create an endogeneity problem. Following Wooldridge (2010, p. 650), two lags are typically used in calculating the Granger causality test in annual data. 

Table 8 presents the results of the Granger causality test. Although the Panel A results indicate a unidirectional causality between aggregate ESG and ROA, we find a bidirectional relationship between aggregate ESG and Econ. Panel B reports the relationship between individual ESG elements and performance, and shows that, in general, there is a unidirectional relationship between the individual ESG dimension and firm performance. As for the environmental dimension, the Granger causality test indicates no significant impact on ROA, but a bidirectional relationship between the social dimension and Econ. The overall results seem to indicate a unidirectional causality between ESG and performance. The results suggest that, on average, a change in ESG has a positive impact on the change in firm performance.

documents.title: The Integration of Conventional Equity Indices with Environmental, Social, and Governance Indices: Evidence from Emerging Economies
documents.snippet:
The environmental, social, and governance equity indices are increasingly popular among investors concerned with sustainable and responsible investment [2]. Firms included on environmental social and governance (ESG) equity indices have to reflect superior sustainability performance and outperform their peers in an in-depth analysis of economics, environment, and social criteria. Based on this, these firms are considered sustainability leaders [12]. Here, we study the newly developed MSCI ESG equity indices in the BRICS countries and examine their integration with their counterpart MSCI composite equity indices in the same countries and across these countries. The unit root diagnostic tests of ADF and PP suggest that all the times-series are stationary at level and at three lags. Further, the Johansen cointegration test confirms long-run integration between the two equity indices in the same country, as well across countries. Moreover, our findings suggest that there is a bi-directional spillover between the MSCI ESG equity indices and the MSCI composite equity indices in the same country, namely the returns of the MSCI ESG indices influence their counterpart composite indices, and vice versa. However, our findings reveal there is no long-run causality between conventional and non-conventional equity indices in the BRICS countries Brazil and Russia, although there is evidence of this in the remaining BRICS countries. Further, there is evidence of short-run causality between MSCI ESG and MSCI composite indices in all BRICS countries. This shows that the non-conventional markets in the BRICS countries are drawing investors, as well as their conventional markets. The short-run and long-run integration of these two indices may also suggest that investors are using the information of one index to predict the behavior of the other. 

It is important to investigate the cross-border financial market integration in the case of the BRICS countries, in particular, due to their economic and financial cooperation. Our study finds that there is long-run causality between MSCI ESG equity indices in one country and the MSCI composite indices of all other BRICS countries. This implies that one country's conventional market flows to the other countries' non-conventional markets. The impulse response analysis also shows that the Brazil and Russia MSCI ESG equity returns respond negatively to one standard deviation shock in their counterpart composite returns for a prolonged period and then stabilize.

documents.title: Linking financial development to environmental performance index—the case of Romania
documents.snippet:
In order to identify cointegration relations, we used Canonical Cointegrating Regression (CCR) proposed by Park's (1992) which is very similar to Fully Modified Least Squares (FMOLS), but instead it applies stationary transformations of the data in order to obtain least squares estimates to remove the long run dependence between the cointegrating equation and stochastic regressors innovations.Estimates based on the CCR are, thus, fully efficient and have the same unbiased, mixture of normal asymptotic as FMOLS.

We used prewhitened Quadratic-spectral kernel estimators of the long-run covariance matrices to estimate the cointegration relations.The first thing we note is that the VAR prewhitening has a strong effect on the kernel part of the calculation of the long-run covariances, shortening the Andrews optimal bandwidth.

As it can be seen from Table 4, all variables included in the model are statistically significant, given the value of the associated probabilities (p-value is 0.0000 for all the variables).The results emphasize a negative influence on the environmental performance index in the case of financial institutions, from the access index and depth index, while in the case of financial markets, the negative impact of the access index of financial markets can be observed.Moreover, the efficiency index, both in the case of financial institutions and financial markets, is generating a positive influence on environmental performance in Romania.The financial markets depth also positively influences the evolution of the environmental performance index.

Considering that the cointegration relations between all the variables included in the model were identified, we highlighted the causal relations between the variables and their direction, through the Pairwise Granger Causality test, in the last stage.Based on the obtained results, we summarized the relationships identified in Figure 3.

According to Figure 3, the evolution of the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) is influencing the evolution of FME and, at the same time, FIA, FIE, FME and  FMA have an impact on the evolution of EPI.Also, it can be noted that the financial development indexes have a higher impact on the development of the financial markets' indexes, while the evolution of the financial markets' development is only influencing the development of the Financial institutions access index (FIA).

documents.title: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Practices and Performance in Shariah Firms: Agency or Stakeholder Theory?
documents.snippet:
This study recognises the possibility of the endogeneity effect between ESG and performance. For example, ESG engagement may lead to higher performance; on the other hand, firms with higher performance are more likely to engage in ESG as they have more financial resources. Graves and Waddock (1994), and Hart and Ahuja (1996), among others, have used lagged ESG as an independent variable. In the previous sections, we have used lagged independent variables for the ESG performance for all the regression models. In this section, we perform the Granger causality test to determine if there is a two-way causality that can create an endogeneity problem. Following Wooldridge (2010, p. 650), two lags are typically used in calculating the Granger causality test in annual data. 

Table 8 presents the results of the Granger causality test. Although the Panel A results indicate a unidirectional causality between aggregate ESG and ROA, we find a bidirectional relationship between aggregate ESG and Econ. Panel B reports the relationship between individual ESG elements and performance, and shows that, in general, there is a unidirectional relationship between the individual ESG dimension and firm performance. As for the environmental dimension, the Granger causality test indicates no significant impact on ROA, but a bidirectional relationship between the social dimension and Econ. The overall results seem to indicate a unidirectional causality between ESG and performance. The results suggest that, on average, a change in ESG has a positive impact on the change in firm performance.

documents.title: The static and dynamic connectedness of environmental, social, and governance investments: International evidence
documents.snippet: The rise of sustainable investing over the last two decades, together with its immense growth potential, have stimulated interest of academics, practitioners, and policy makers. It is important to analyze performance of ESG markets during major economic and financial shocks, especially during turbulent time-periods. This paper examines the co- Z. Umar et al. Economic Modelling 93 (2020) 112-124 movement and transmissions between ESG indices and a set of influential macroeconomic and financial variables for the period ranging from 10/ 1/2007-04/15/2020. MSCI ESG Leaders Indices are selected for the ten most significant ESG markets worldwide. We employ four global risk factors; the VIX volatility index, the US Economic Policy Uncertainty index, the WTI crude oil price and changes in the US 10-year Treasury bond yield. We employ a two-fold methodology. Firstly, we use the Granger (1969) causality approach to evaluate the causality between the employed variables. Subsequently, the connectedness between these variables is assessed by using the Diebold and Yilmaz (2012) methodology. This approach enables us to estimate the magnitude and the direction of spillovers across the various variables, as well as to identify any transmission channels. Our empirical results show significant transmissions between the selected ESG indices throughout our sample period from 10/1/2007-04/ 15/2020.
